title: Rudy Giuliani, Ex-New York Mayor Who Helped Trump Overturn His 2020 Defeat, Gets Medal Of Freedom
description: Trump announced he would honor Giuliani, 82, in September 2025 shortly after the former mayor was badly injured in a car accident.
author: Reuters
content:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday awarded the Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian honor, to Rudy Giuliani, the former New York mayor who became a national figure after the September 11, 2001, attacks and later helped Trump try to overturn his 2020 election defeat.
Trump announced he would honor Giuliani, 82, in September 2025 shortly after the former mayor was badly injured in a car accident. Trump at the time called him "the greatest Mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot."
After the 9/11 attacks, Giuliani became one of the most popular figures in US politics. He launched a Republican presidential bid in 2007, and even after it failed, he remained a prominent conservative messenger.
In a statement, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales called Giuliani "a dedicated public servant whose decisive leadership has left a lasting impact on New York City and our nation."
Trump awarded the medal in a private Oval Office ceremony.
Giuliani in a statement said he was "honored and humbled" by the medal, and credited advice from President Ronald Reagan, under whom he served as associate attorney general and a US Attorney, for guiding his public service.
"I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me - particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together," Giuliani said.
His son, former Trump administration official Andrew Giuliani, told reporters outside the White House that the ceremony was a "special" gathering in which Trump and Giuliani reminisced about their long friendship.
Their alliance deepened after Trump lost the 2020 election. Giuliani advanced falsehoods about the result and the integrity of the voting process. He held a press conference at a Philadelphia landscaping business, where he made claims that were widely rebutted, then another at the headquarters of the Republican National Committee where hair dye dribbled down his face.
His false claims came with legal consequences. He was barred from practicing law in New York, where he once served as the US Attorney in the state's southern district, and Washington, and faced criminal charges in Georgia and Arizona for attempting to subvert the 2020 election results.
Two Georgia election workers won a $148 million judgment against Giuliani in December 2023 for defamation. He "fully satisfied" the terms of the judgment in February 2025.
By the end of that year, Trump pardoned him for federal criminal offenses.
With Giuliani's medal, Trump has awarded the Medal of Freedom 27 times between his two terms. He has predominantly reserved the honor -- designated by President John F. Kennedy for "meritorious contribution" to US security or national interests, world peace or cultural endeavors -- for former athletes. Fourteen of Trump's awards have been to retired athletes, some of whom also served in public office.
He has said he plans to award the medal to retired and scandal-plagued Major League Baseball pitcher Roger Clemens and US national hockey team goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.
Trump posthumously awarded the medal to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk in October 2025.

title: Author Of 'How To Kill A Federal Judge' Sentenced To 6.5 Years For Threats
description: US District Judge Karen Schreier during a hearing in St Paul sentenced Robert Phillip Ivers, 73, after a jury in August found him guilty of mailing threatening communications and threatening to murder a federal judge.
author: Reuters
content:
A Minnesota man was sentenced on Tuesday to 6-1/2 years in prison after his conviction for writing and distributing a 236-page manuscript titled "How to Kill a Federal Judge" that threatened numerous people, including a judge who presided over an earlier, similar case against him.
US District Judge Karen Schreier during a hearing in St Paul sentenced Robert Phillip Ivers, 73, after a jury in August found him guilty of mailing threatening communications and threatening to murder a federal judge.
Prosecutors had sought a sentence at the high end of the recommended 97- to 121-month range he faced, saying Ivers' conduct was not an isolated incident and that a message needed to be sent after the number of hostile threats and communications targeting federal judges more than tripled over a decade.
"Ivers's sentence should make crystal clear that such threats of violence cannot and will not be normalized," prosecutors in a court filing told Schreier, who sits in South Dakota but was assigned the case after all the federal judges in Minnesota recused themselves.
Ivers' court-appointed attorney did not respond to a request for comment. In court papers, he asked the judge to show Ivers leniency, citing health concerns.
Ivers, who was previously convicted of threatening to kill a federal judge in 2019, was arrested in September 2025 after staff at a library in Wayzata, Minnesota, reported seeing him print copies of his manuscript.
Prosecutors alleged Ivers gave staff a three-page flyer that described his book as a guide "designed to teach extremists on how to plan, train, hunt, stalk and kill anyone including judges, their family members, politicians and more!"
Authorities said they later found 20 spiral-bound copies of the manuscript in his car.
Prosecutors called the document a "manifesto" and said it named multiple individuals and judges. Between January and April 2025, Ivers mailed copies to all nine US Supreme Court justices, three federal appeals judges, a law firm and a university, prosecutors said.
The document included threats to kill Iowa-based US District Judge Robert Pratt, who before his death in January had, due to recusals by Minnesota judges, presided over a 2019 trial in which Ivers was convicted of threatening to kill US District Judge Wilhelmina Wright.
Pratt sentenced Ivers to 18 months in prison. Prosecutors said that Ivers' manuscript threatened Pratt as well as a lawyer who had testified to hearing Ivers threaten to kill Wright.
"Begging for your life won't do you one bit of good judge," Ivers wrote regarding Pratt, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors initially also charged Ivers with threatening to kill a Supreme Court justice but later dropped that charge.
The case is United States v. Ivers, US District Court for the District of Minnesota, No. 25-cr-00347.

title: ‘Are we beggars?’ Congress fumes as Akhilesh offers 26 seats for UP polls
description: NEW DELHI: Tensions between the \"UP ke do ladke\" appear to be spilling into the open, with UP Congress working president Imran Masood making his
author: Abhishek Mishra
content:
Congress MP's outburst after Akhilesh offers 26 seats (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Tensions between the "UP ke do ladke" appear to be spilling into the open, with UP Congress working president Imran Masood making his displeasure clear after Samajwadi Party announced its first list of candidates for upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections."Are we beggars?" Congress MP Masood asked, expressing his strong objection over Akhilesh Yadav's decision to offer Congress just 26 "winnable" seats even as seat-sharing negotiations between the two INDIA bloc allies remain under way.
The sharp reaction from Masood comes at a time when Congress and Samajwadi Party are still trying to work out an alliance for the upcoming polls. The SP's announcement of its first list of five candidates, largely from western Uttar Pradesh, appears to have added friction to the already delicate negotiations."Where is the alliance? If you are acting like this, then where is the alliance? Our leadership will decide what we need to do; I just don't understand it. Here you say one thing, and there something else happens," Masood told news agency IANS.Making it clear that the final call would rest with the Congress leadership, the MP said he would abide by whatever decision the party takes."This decision has to be taken by our party. What Akhilesh Ji is doing or not doing is not a big issue for me; I am bound by my party, and whatever my party says, I have to do that," he said.
Referring to the upcoming visits of senior Congress leaders Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi, Masood said party workers would abide by the directions issued by the leadership."Rahul Gandhi will come, Priyanka Gandhi will come, and whatever instructions our leadership gives us, we have to follow them. SP's announcement makes no difference to us. However, it must definitely be decided whether the fight is against the BJP or against the Congress," he said.The immediate flashpoint is the SP's reported offer of 26 "winnable" constituencies to the Congress, against the latter's reported demand for around 130 seats. Masood said the Congress had not even formally demanded seats from its ally before the SP announced its offer."I don't understand it. It's beyond my understanding; the party has to take a decision on this, I don't understand. Are we beggars? Will you treat us like this- that we aren't even asking you for seats and you declared 26 seats? We didn't even demand seats from you. So if this is your way of working, that you will dictate terms, then a self-respecting person like me does not understand these things," he said.Taking a direct swipe at the SP leadership, Masood added, "You don't care about the alliance anyway. You are just running your own party, so go ahead and run your party- we aren't stopping or doing anything to you."Meanwhile, Congress leader Udit Raj said, "A great deal of permutation and combination is required in Uttar Pradesh; factors like political chemistry, winnability, and the choice of candidates will all be taken into account."The outburst follows a 3.5-hour meeting between the two parties in New Delhi on Tuesday as negotiations over seat-sharing for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections continued. While both sides claimed progress, no breakthrough was announced.
Meanwhile, SP has maintained that winnability would be the key factor in deciding the seat-sharing arrangement.After announcing its first list, Akhilesh Yadav said the party had offered Congress 26 constituencies it considered winnable and indicated that discussions would continue.
"The winning start has been made with the first ‘26 seats’. Working together wisely, things will move forward." he posted in Hindi on X.
Congress draws red line at 120 seats in UP
Congress has sought 120 seats in the upcoming polls during seat-sharing talks with Samajwadi Party and is "unwilling to settle for fewer", party sources told news agency ANI.Congress submitted a list of 120 constituencies during a meeting with SP leaders in Delhi. The list reportedly includes two seats in Saharanpur, where the SP has already announced candidates, as well as constituencies in Rae Bareli and Amethi, some of which have sitting SP MLAs.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

title: 'Lot of runs here': Forget the seamer-friendly reputation, New Zealand pacer says Hagley Oval pitch can flatten out
description: New Zealand pacer Matt Henry has cautioned against reading too much into Hagley Oval's reputation as a seamer-friendly venue ahead of the second Test
author: Shubhanshu Dwivedi
content:
New Zealand pacer 
Matt Henry
 has cautioned against reading too much into Hagley Oval's reputation as a seamer-friendly venue ahead of the second Test against India, which begins in Christchurch on Friday. The warning comes after the opening Test in Wellington turned into a batting-dominated contest despite expectations of assistance for fast bowlers.
Only 24 wickets fell across five days in the drawn first Test, with India scoring 720 in their second innings, their highest total overseas. India captain Shubman Gill had expressed his disappointment with the pitch after the teams shook hands with more than 15 overs remaining on the final day.
Henry, who has enjoyed success at Hagley Oval, said New Zealand would wait to see how the surface behaves rather than make plans based on its reputation.
"I think every game's different, every surface you play on is slightly different as well. And I think there's been a lot of runs scored here of late as well," Henry said at a press conference on Wednesday.
"So for us, it's probably not to get carried away with what it could be and trying to read pitches. 
It's a pretty fine art to do that."
There is reason for New Zealand to be cautious about the conditions. India A and New Zealand A played a four-day match at the venue earlier this month, which also ended in a draw after both teams scored heavily.
New Zealand A made 424 in their first innings, with Matt Boyle scoring 110, in reply to India A's 346, which included Dhruv Jurel's 105. India A then scored 282 for two in their second innings, with Yashasvi Jaiswal unbeaten on 155, as the pitch became easier for batting.
Henry acknowledged that Hagley Oval has traditionally offered help to fast bowlers, particularly through bounce and carry. However, he said batting conditions can improve as a match progresses.
"I think traditionally here in New Zealand, the wickets when there's grass on them tend to get better and better, and it's been the same here. It's a good batting venue. Obviously, when there's bounce involved, it's good for the bowler, but from a batting point of view you can score runs quickly as well," he said.
The 34-year-old also said batters would need to rely on their defence during difficult periods before looking to score freely.
"There's moments where you probably have to rely on your defence a little bit, but when you get through those periods, you really can put bowlers under pressure because, like you said, when it flattens out, your margins become pretty small as a bowler."
Henry added that playing at home gives New Zealand a degree of familiarity with the ground, though the team would still have to assess the conditions during the match.
"It's always nice when you're at home and it is a ground you've played a lot of cricket at, so you probably have that element of comfort. You kind of know the ground well and whatnot.
"But yeah, it's been a great place to play cricket in the past, somewhere I love to play cricket."

title: Meerut woman escapes hotel after night of assault, ex-boyfriend catches her, drags her back in crowded market
description: MEERUT: A 24-year-old woman allegedly escaped from a hotel room in Meerut on Tuesday but was caught by her former boyfriend, who tried to drag her back.
author: Sandeep Rai
content:
MEERUT: A 24-year-old woman allegedly escaped from a hotel room in Meerut on Tuesday but was caught by her former boyfriend, who tried to drag her back. The incident, which took place in the busy Abu Lane market, was captured on CCTV.
The accused, identified as Mohd Salman, allegedly chased the woman, caught hold of her and attempted to take her back to the hotel. He fled across the rooftop after police reached the spot following alerts from passersby.
According to police, the woman, a resident of Vasundhara in Ghaziabad, had known Salman, a resident of Jainpur village in Meerut's Rohta area, for around two-and-a-half years. The two were previously in a relationship. Her family has recently arranged her marriage elsewhere.
The woman told police that she had visited a friend in Mohkampur on Monday. While she was returning to Ghaziabad later that night, Salman allegedly took her to a hotel on Abu Lane, assaulted her and confined her to a room overnight. He also snatched her phone, which he returned later, she alleged.
In her FIR, registered on Tuesday night, the woman stated: "Salman was my boyfriend a year ago. 
On Monday, I came to meet a friend in Mohkampur. While I was returning to Ghaziabad at night, Salman took me from my friend's place to a hotel, thrashed me and confined me there. He even snatched away my phone, though he returned it later. I escaped on Tuesday afternoon, but he caught hold of me, threatened me and then fled."
Salman has been booked under sections 115(2), 127(2) and 351(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), relating to voluntarily causing hurt, wrongful confinement and criminal intimidation.
"A man and a woman had checked into a hotel. Following an argument, violence broke out between them. The woman told us that she had known the youth for the past two-and-a-half years and clarified that she had not been abducted. Teams have been constituted based on her complaint, and strict action will be taken against the accused," said Circle Officer (Sadar) Sanjay Gupta.
Police have sealed the hotel and formed two teams, including the SWAT unit, to conduct raids and apprehend Salman.

title: IBM to H-1B visa and green card holders in its biggest division: You can leave the company by end of 2026 as we are ending...
description: IBM is ending US visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting, its biggest division with more than 150,000 employees.
author: TOI Tech Desk
content:
IBM
 is ending US visa and green card sponsorship for most roles in IBM Consulting, its biggest division with more than 150,000 employees. Workers affected by the change can either move to an IBM role outside the US or leave the company by the end of the year, Bloomberg first reported, citing a document shared with managers in the unit.
The company has confirmed the decision. "IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages," an IBM spokesperson said, adding that this participation had been declining for a number of years. "As skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting."
IBM's H-1B workers get three weeks to choose between relocating and leaving
The choice is not an easy one. Employees get three weeks to decide, according to Sunguk Moon, CEO of anonymous workplace forum Blind. Those who don't take a role abroad get three months of severance, with December 31 as their last day. Many heard about it in what was set up as a one-on-one "career sync" with their manager.
Relocating comes with its own price. One IBM employee wrote on Blind that moving to India could mean a pay cut of roughly 80%.
Most of the openings are in one country too. On November 19, IBM's careers portal listed 1,278 consulting roles outside the US, of which 1,125 were in India, 23 in Singapore and 18 in the UK. 
The US had 89.
IBM does not share how its workforce is split by country, so the exact number of people affected is unclear. Federal records show the company had just over 1,600 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal year 2026, down from over 2,000 in FY2025 and nearly 3,000 in FY2024. These numbers cover all of IBM, not only consulting, and include extensions for existing staff.
Trump administration's H-1B visa crackdown is reshaping how tech companies hire
The move comes amid tight scrutiny of foreign tech hiring by the Donald Trump administration. Last month, it suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several major outsourcers, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process, Reuters reported. PERM is a key step for companies sponsoring foreign workers for green cards. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced the suspensions, and Microsoft has publicly defended its hiring of international talent.
In September 2025, the White House announced a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, though the measure has since been tied up in the courts. The administration has also proposed changes to the annual H-1B lottery that would favour employers paying the highest salaries.
Indian professionals stand to feel this the most. Indian nationals typically receive about three-quarters of all H-1B visas, and their wait for a green card can stretch to several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy.
IBM Consulting's flat growth sits behind the sponsorship cut
Over the past few years, IBM has rebuilt itself as a software company through big acquisitions such as Red Hat, HashiCorp and Confluent. Consulting, by far its largest unit, has not kept up. The division's growth has been largely flat since 2024, as per Bloomberg, and its revenue stayed at $5.3 billion in the third quarter, up 2% at constant currency.
IBM's 2025 annual report put the company's total headcount at 264,300 employees across IBM and its wholly owned subsidiaries.

title: World Chess Championship: Sindarov says 'Indian chess players are always meditating' after first game draw with Gukesh
description: Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov made an interesting observation about Indian chess players when asked about the psychological state of his opponent, D
author: Shubhanshu Dwivedi
content:
Uzbekistan's Javokhir Sindarov made an interesting observation about Indian chess players when asked about the psychological state of his opponent, D Gukesh, after their opening game of the FIDE World Championship in Geneva ended in a drwa on Tuesday. "I saw that all the players from India are always meditating," Sindarov said, adding that he had noticed the habit while playing against Gukesh, R Praggnanandhaa and Arjun Erigaisi.
The remark came during the post-match press conference after defending champion Gukesh, playing with black, drew the first game against the Uzbek challenger. The two players were also asked about how they read each other's behaviour at the board, with Sindarov pointing to Gukesh closing his eyes and Indian players meditating.
"I do it in every tournament; it's not just here. And also, I saw that all the players from India are always meditating, which for me is okay. I played many times with Arjun, Pragg, and Gukesh; maybe not many, but whenever we meet, he is also meditating. So nothing special here," Sindarov said.
Gukesh, meanwhile, said the two players had similar habits and that their actions at the board were not necessarily signs of nerves.
"I don't know, maybe there were a little bit of nerves also, but I think both of our habits are similar. In general, he taps his foot or shakes his leg, and I close my eyes, in any tournament, not just the match. It's just how we behave at the board," the Indian said.
On the board, Gukesh had to work his way back after Sindarov gained a small advantage in the early stages. The Indian chose the Berlin Defence against Sindarov's Ruy Lopez, and was under some pressure before the game moved into a queen-less middle game.
Sindarov had better-placed pieces and a slightly better pawn structure for a period, but the Uzbek sacrificed a pawn to open up the position. Gukesh, however, found the right moves despite being short of time. At one point, the Indian appeared to have a chance to take control, but Sindarov held his position and repeated the moves.
The position was repeated five times before the players agreed to a draw. A threefold repetition is usually enough to claim a draw.
Asked how it felt to finally play after all the build-up to the championship, Gukesh said the actual game was the easiest part of the process.
"That was the easiest thing, to actually go and play the game, because there's so much thinking, so much work to do before that. Once you get to the game, you know, it's like your home."
He also said he was not worried despite getting into time trouble, as he had already considered his next moves.
"I thought I was always under control, not in a place where I really needed to be worried. When I got into time trouble, I had already thought about the next few moves, what I was going to play soon. I was happy that I managed to spend some time, find a good solution, and the moves after that were pretty easy."
The two players will contest 14 classical games, with the first to reach 7.5 points winning the title. If the scores are level after 14 games, shorter-format games will be played to decide the champion. Gukesh will have the white pieces in the second game.
The time control allows 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, with 30 seconds added for every move from move 41. Players cannot agree to a draw before 40 moves, although a game can end earlier through threefold repetition or stalemate.
The total prize fund for the match is USD 2.5 million. Each win is worth USD 200,000, with the remaining amount to be split equally between the players. If the match goes to tie-breaks, the winner will receive USD 1.3 million and the runner-up USD 1.2 million.

title: A study of 18,457 skeletons from 45 countries found people got shorter for centuries as farming and technology spread, with men in Southeast Asia losing about 7 inches by the 1800s
description: If you are short-heighted, you have technology to blame for that. Well, at least some of it.
author: TOI Science Desk
content:
If you are short-heighted, you have technology to blame for that. Well, at least some of it.
New research has found that as farming and technology spread across societies, people in several parts of the world gradually became shorter. In fact, men in Southeast Asia, who averaged around 5 feet 10 inches about 7,000 years ago, were barely over 5 feet 3 inches by the 1800s. That is a difference of nearly seven inches!
The findings come from 
a study of 18,457 skeletons from 45 countries
, which suggests that technological advancement did not necessarily translate into better living conditions for the people benefiting from it.
The study conducted
Image Courtesy: Baten et al. (2026), PNAS
Published in the journal 
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS),
 the study was conducted by researchers from the University of Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. The team examined 18,457 skeletal remains collected from 783 archaeological sites across Europe and Asia, dating back approximately 7,000 years.
But how do you figure out how tall someone was thousands of years ago, when all that remains of them are their bones?
The researchers used the femur, or thighbone, to estimate the height of individuals. Since the femur is one of the longest bones in the human body and its length is closely related to overall stature, it can provide a fairly reliable estimate of how tall someone was during their lifetime.
Height is also more than just a physical characteristic. While genetics play an important role, childhood nutrition, access to food and exposure to diseases can determine how much a person grows. Children who do not receive adequate nutrition or repeatedly suffer from infections may not reach their full growth potential. This makes average height a useful indicator of the general health and living conditions of a population.
By comparing these estimates across different periods, the researchers found that average human height declined in most of the regions studied between 500 and 1900 CE. Interestingly, this happened alongside considerable technological and agricultural development.
The case of Southeast Asia
We often note that men in Southeast Asian countries are shorter than those in several other parts of the world. In fact, 
recent estimates by Our World in Data
 put the average height of men in Singapore at around 173.5 cm (5 feet 8 inches), while Thailand follows at 171.6 cm (5 feet 7.5 inches). In comparison, men in Indonesia average around 165.3 cm (5 feet 5 inches), while those in the Philippines average approximately 163.5 cm (5 feet 4 inches). These figures are based on country-wise estimates for young adults and vary depending on the population and age group being measured.
However, what makes this region particularly interesting is how much average height appears to have changed over thousands of years.
According to the study
, men in the region averaged approximately 1.78 metres (5 feet 10 inches) around 7,000 years ago. By the 19th century, this had fallen to just over 1.60 metres (approximately 5 feet 3 inches). That is a difference of nearly 18 centimetres!
So, why did people become shorter as societies developed?
The researchers believe population growth may have played an important role. Agricultural innovations allowed communities to produce more food, but they also made it possible to support larger populations. As more people settled in one place and depended on the same resources, the benefits of increased food production were not necessarily shared equally.
China offers an interesting example. During the 11th century, the introduction of higher-yielding rice varieties and other agricultural innovations increased food production. While this helped support a growing population, it did not necessarily improve the nutritional quality of people's diets.
In fact, as the population grew, individuals had fewer resources available to them. People might have had enough food to survive, but their diets could lack important nutrients, particularly high-quality protein. Over generations, this could have affected how tall children grew.
It is worth noting that technology did not make everyone shorter. Northern Europe, for instance, experienced an increase in average height following the spread of dairy farming. Greater consumption of dairy products, alongside the spread of lactose tolerance, helped improve nutrition. Height trends varied considerably depending on the region, available food and living conditions.
The study does not suggest that technological advancement or the introduction of farming was necessarily bad for humanity. After all, these developments helped societies grow, support larger populations and eventually build the world we live in today. However, they also reveal an interesting contradiction: a society can become more productive without necessarily making life better for everyone living in it.

title: ‘Not a single bogus vote to be added’: Akhilesh tells SP workers to monitor election commission activities
description: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday urged the party's 'PDA sentinels' across Uttar Pradesh to monitor the Election Commission's
author: Pranjal Pandey
content:
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday urged the party's 'PDA sentinels' across Uttar Pradesh to monitor the Election Commission's electoral roll activities ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections.In a post on X, Yadav asked party workers across the state to remain vigilant about the poll body's activities, with two principles for monitoring changes to voter lists: "Not a single bogus vote to be added, not a single genuine vote to be removed!"The SP chief also raised concerns over the credibility of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), referring to public scepticism about the voting system.
"How can we trust them, when ‘Haathi ke daant khaane ke aur, dikhaane keaur’ (All show, no substance)," Yadav said.In his post, the party chief also mentioned the controversy surrounding the Chandigarh mayoral election, referring to what he called the BJP's 'Chandigarh trick'. He said people were aware of the episode and understood such political tactics.The Chandigarh mayoral election controversy centres on allegations of deliberate ballot tampering by presiding officer Anil Masih during the January 30, 2024, mayoral polls. The Supreme Court subsequently found that Masih had deliberately marked eight ballot papers cast in favour of Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)-Congress candidate Kuldeep Kumar, leading to their wrongful rejection. Later, the apex court quashed the initially declared result and declared Kumar the validly elected mayor of Chandigarh.On Tuesday, Yadav urged the Congress to identify more potential constituencies beyond the 26 seats on its priority list as the two parties negotiate a seat-sharing arrangement for Assembly elections, ANI reported.
He said the discussions should be conducted in the name of the INDIA alliance rather than being limited to candidates from either the Samajwadi Party or the Congress. Yadav described the two parties' cooperation as a "historic opportunity" to defeat what he called the "communal BJP and its narrow-minded allies".
He called for serious discussions that take public expectations and political realities into account, saying the alliance should aim to win in as many constituencies as possible."Among the seats you and we contest, the number we win should exceed the number we lose. Only victory will make the division of seats respectable, because only the seats we win will bring us respect," he said.Yadav also asked the Congress to share the names of all other constituencies it considered winnable, apart from the 26 already discussed. He said both parties could then assess the prospects of potential candidates in each seat.
Pranjal Pandey is a journalist with the editorial desk of The Times of India (Online). He looks at the implications of global events for India, with a particular interest in geopolitics and defence. You can sometimes find him looking at the world map, wondering what’s new.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks execution delay, says he was defending Taliban
description: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban
author: Prisha Patnaik
content:
Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.
In a court filing signed by Hasan on Tuesday, he said he intended to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his death sentence had been obtained and were being maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.
The filing could delay the Trump administration’s plans to execute Hasan on December 3. A hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday morning.
Hasan, who is representing himself with assistance from lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union’s Capital Punishment Project, said he intended to continue representing himself in the legal fight.
Hasan wants to revive defence barred at trial
One of Hasan’s central arguments is that he was prevented from presenting a defence that his actions were legally justified because he was trying to protect the Afghan Taliban from what he described as an unlawful attack by the US Army.
Hasan had argued that he was acting in “defense of others”, according to court documents. However, the military judge barred him from presenting that argument during his 2013 trial.
After dismissing his lawyers and choosing to represent himself, Hasan largely remained silent during the three-week trial. 
While the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan called none in his defence and made no closing argument.
A military jury found him guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder for the shooting, which left 13 people dead and 32 wounded.
The case has been assigned to US district judge Tony Mattivi in Kansas, where Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth. Mattivi was nominated by president Donald Trump and confirmed by the Senate in June.
What happened in the Fort Hood attack?
On November 5, 2009, Hasan walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers were waiting for medical tests and preparing for deployment.
He opened fire with a handgun fitted with laser sights, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.
Hasan was shot by law enforcement officers during the attack, leaving him paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.
He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death.
Execution controversy and survivors’ objections
Trump authorised Hasan’s execution on the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II and the first military execution since 1961.
The plan drew controversy after Hegseth announced that the execution would be public and the Pentagon confirmed it would be livestreamed. Critics from both parties raised concerns that broadcasting the execution could fuel radicalisation and turn it into a spectacle.
Trump later said the execution would not be livestreamed, but that immediate family members of the victims could witness it in person if they chose.
The latest court filing comes amid further dispute over who will be allowed to attend. Military officials have denied requests from three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations, security and space constraints.
The survivors argued that the military should recognise them as victims under a broader definition that includes direct physical, emotional or financial harm. The Army rejected their appeal, saying regulations specify who may attend a military execution.

title: At England's famous Sutton Hoo burial ground, archaeologists uncovered a ghost-like outline of an Anglo-Saxon body in sand, with beads, a knife and a brooch, plus signs that another grave lies below
description: Imagine excavating a centuries-old grave, brushing away layers of sand and soil, only to find the outline of a person staring back at you.
author: TOI Science Desk
content:
Imagine excavating a centuries-old grave, brushing away layers of sand and soil, only to find the outline of a person staring back at you. There are no bones, no skull and no remains of the body itself. Yet, somehow, its shape is still there, preserved in the sand like a ghost that never quite left.
This is what 
National Trust archaeologists have uncovered at Sutton Hoo
, one of England's most famous Anglo-Saxon burial sites. The discovery of a rare 'sand body', accompanied by beads, a knife, tweezers and a brooch, is offering researchers a glimpse into the lives of people who lived more than a thousand years ago. Even more intriguingly, the excavation has revealed signs that another person may have been buried directly beneath it, raising the possibility of a double burial.
When the body disappears, but its shape remains
The discovery might sound like something straight out of a ghost story, but there is a fascinating explanation behind it. The sand bodies are a result of the unusual conditions in which these people were buried, as 
National Trust UK explains
.
Over hundreds of years, the acidic soil gradually dissolved the bones and soft tissues of the deceased. However, as the body decomposed, the surrounding sand retained its shape, eventually hardening into a solid impression of the person who had once occupied that space. 
What remains is not an actual skeleton or a preserved corpse, but a negative impression of a human body.
National Trust archaeologist Angus Wainwright
 explained in the announcement that these burials were found during earlier excavations at Sutton Hoo in the 1980s. The bodies and bones had disappeared into the acidic soil, leaving behind hard sand that retained their form. He compared the unusual discovery to some of the bodies found at Pompeii, although the preservation process is different.
Finding another such burial gives archaeologists an opportunity to study a person whose physical remains would otherwise have been lost entirely. The outline can offer clues about how the individual was laid to rest, while the objects buried alongside them provide a little more information about the life they might have led.
A grave that tells a story through its belongings
While the sand body itself is remarkable, the objects found alongside it are just as interesting. Archaeologists recovered beads, a pair of tweezers, a knife and a brooch, all of which could help researchers understand the person who was buried there.
Grave goods were an important part of burial practices in early Anglo-Saxon communities. Objects were often placed alongside the deceased, reflecting aspects of their identity, clothing, daily life or the status they held within their community. Jewellery, for instance, could offer clues about how someone dressed, while tools and other personal belongings could tell researchers something about the world they inhabited.
The brooch and beads show how people dressed and adorned themselves. The knife and tweezers, meanwhile, add to the collection of everyday objects that accompanied the individual into the grave. Although it is difficult to establish exactly who the person was from these belongings alone, they offer a starting point for understanding a life that has otherwise disappeared from the archaeological record.
There is also evidence from elsewhere in Garden Field that suggests the cemetery may have belonged to a community experiencing changes in wealth and social standing. A gold ingot discovered during the wider excavations has raised questions about whether some of the people buried here were accumulating wealth and gaining influence.
Sutton Hoo is best known for its extraordinary royal burial, but its surrounding landscape was also home to ordinary people who lived, worked and raised families in the region. Their graves may not contain the same extravagant treasures, but they can tell us just as much about how Anglo-Saxon society functioned.
Beyond the famous royal burial ground
Time Team at Sutton Hoo | Image Courtesy: James Dobson/National Trust Images
Located near Woodbridge in Suffolk, England, Sutton Hoo became internationally famous in 1939, when archaeologists uncovered an extraordinary Anglo-Saxon ship burial beneath one of its burial mounds.
The 27-metre-long ship had been used as a burial chamber, containing an impressive collection of objects, including a helmet, a sword, a shield, gold ornaments and silverware. The discovery transformed what historians knew about early medieval England, revealing the wealth, craftsmanship and international connections of the Anglo-Saxon world.
The burial is widely associated with King Rædwald of East Anglia, who is believed to have died around AD 627, although his identity has never been conclusively established.
For decades, much of the archaeological attention at Sutton Hoo has centred on these royal burial mounds and the powerful people who were laid to rest there. The recent excavations in Garden Field, however, are helping researchers look beyond the kings and their treasures.
According to Wainwright in the announcement
, the landscape surrounding the royal burial ground was equally familiar to the everyday East Anglians who lived in the villages and farms of the river valley. The latest excavation shifts attention towards these communities, their ancestors and their descendants.
The Garden Field cemetery could therefore help researchers understand who lived in the region, how they buried their dead and whether they had connections to the people associated with Sutton Hoo's royal mounds. It is a reminder that history is not only shaped by the people who ruled, but also by the communities who lived alongside them.
Another mystery lies beneath the sand body
As if discovering a human-shaped outline without a human body were not intriguing enough, archaeologists have another mystery to investigate. Evidence found directly beneath the sand body suggests that a second individual may have been buried in the same grave.
Whether the two people were buried together or at different points in time is not yet clear. They could have shared a family connection, or the grave might have been reused after an earlier burial. Researchers will need to examine the evidence more closely before drawing any conclusions about their relationship.
The discovery also adds to questions surrounding the different burial practices found across Sutton Hoo. Some individuals were cremated, while others were buried with their bodies intact. The reasons behind these choices, and what they might reveal about the communities living in the area, remain subjects of investigation.
Archaeologists are also continuing to study the Bromeswell Bucket, a sixth-century Byzantine vessel discovered during the earlier 2024 excavation at Garden Field. The bucket was found to contain a cremation burial and grave goods, adding another layer to the site's complicated history.
For Dr Helen Geake, Time Team's Anglo-Saxon specialist, there are still several unanswered questions about the cemetery, she explains in the 
joint press release
. This includes the date of the bucket, the choice between cremation and burial, and the significance of the possible second individual beneath the newly discovered sand body.
The excavations are part of a wider research project between the National Trust and Time Team, which has spent two seasons investigating Garden Field. The findings are being presented in a new four-part documentary series, with the first episode released on YouTube on November 14, 2026.
For now, the ghostly outline in the sand remains one of the most intriguing discoveries from the excavation. There are no bones to identify, no face to recognise and no name to attach to the person who was buried there. Yet, through the shape left behind and the belongings placed alongside them, archaeologists are slowly piecing together a life that might otherwise have been forgotten.

title: Punjab teacher spent 18 years planting around 10,000 trees along roads, schools and public spaces, starting with 125 saplings watered by bucket; at 56, Ranjit Singh Chinna now uses a tractor to keep his mission alive
description: What began with 125 saplings, a bucket of water and a simple concern for children walking under the scorching summer sun has grown into an extraordinary
author: TOI Lifestyle Desk
content:
What began with 125 saplings, a bucket of water and a simple concern for children walking under the scorching summer sun has grown into an extraordinary 18-year mission. At 56, Ranjit Singh Chinna, a government schoolteacher from Punjab's Gurdaspur district, has planted and nurtured around 10,000 fruit-bearing and medicinal trees across highways, village roads and public spaces.
Popularly known as the 'Tree Man of Gurdaspur', Chinna has spent nearly two decades making roads greener, creating shaded spaces and improving his surroundings. His journey has not been driven by a large organisation or an elaborate environmental campaign. Instead, it has been powered by personal commitment, his own resources and the belief that even small efforts can make a difference.
Today, his plantation work extends across several parts of the border district, while his contribution to society goes beyond planting trees. From cleaning public spaces to respectfully burying dead animals and birds found along roads, he has made community service an important part of his life.
A road without trees gave birth to a green mission
Chinna's journey began in 2007 when he noticed something missing along the road connecting his native village, Chinna Railwala, with Naushera Magha Singh. The approximately one-kilometre stretch had no trees, leaving children returning from school and college exposed to the harsh summer heat. 
Rather than waiting for someone else to address the problem, he decided to do something himself.
He planted 125 saplings along the road over three months. However, planting them was only the beginning. With no proper water supply available, he carried water in a bucket and watered each sapling himself. Recalling those early days, Chinna told The New Indian Express, “This road is around one kilometre, so I planted 125 trees in the span of three months and then used to water them with my own bucket, as I had no source to water them otherwise.”
The modest beginning gradually developed into a much larger environmental effort. What started as an attempt to provide shade to children became a lifelong commitment to improving the district's green cover.
From a bucket to a tractor, the work kept growing
As the number of saplings increased, manually carrying water became increasingly difficult. Chinna came up with a practical solution by installing a 500-litre water tank on his motorcycle, using a tyre as its base. This allowed him to transport water and irrigate more plants. However, a back problem eventually made it difficult for him to continue using the motorcycle for the task. He then shifted the water tank to his tractor trolley, which he now uses to water the trees.
Explaining the change, he said, “After that, due to my back problem, I have installed that tank in my tractor trolley and thus now irrigate the plants.” Over the years, his plantation efforts expanded beyond national highways to village link roads and public spaces. He has planted trees around railway stations, schools, cremation grounds and bus stands.
He particularly focuses on planting saplings between June and August. Whenever he identifies suitable land for plantation, he raises around 400 to 500 saplings. The effort requires considerable personal investment, with Chinna spending approximately Rs 60,000 to Rs 65,000 every year on his green mission.
His idea of service extends beyond planting trees
For Chinna, environmental responsibility does not end with making an area greener. He has also taken up several tasks that many people might overlook, including clearing unwanted vegetation and ensuring that dead animals and birds found along roads are properly buried. For the past 15 years, he has been involved in collecting and burying animal and bird carcasses. He considers this an important responsibility because decomposing bodies can create public health concerns and attract harmful bacteria and other pathogens.
He also believes that leaving dead animals exposed or throwing them into garbage dumps is disrespectful. In his view, animals deserve dignity even after death. Explaining why he undertakes this work, Chinna said that removing carcasses also helps prevent accidents, as motorists sometimes make sudden manoeuvres to avoid bodies lying on busy roads. During the rainy season, he additionally clears congress grass along village link roads. His efforts also include cleaning stretches used by devotees after religious processions.
His commitment to public service was visible even before his tree-planting initiative began. According to The Tribune, between 2005 and 2012, he served drinking water to passengers at Chhina railway station every day, without missing a single day. During the Covid-19 pandemic, he also offered to transport infected patients to hospitals using his vehicle.
The 'Tree Man of Gurdaspur' believes small efforts matter
Chinna's dedication has earned him recognition from several social and voluntary organisations. He has also received the Bhai Kanhaiya Award for excellence in social service. Despite the appreciation, he believes the real reward lies in helping others rather than receiving awards. His guiding thought is a simple question: “What are you doing for others?”
He also recognises that one individual cannot transform an entire district's environment alone. According to The Tribune, Gurdaspur has limited forest cover, and Chinna believes greater participation from NGOs and social organisations could help expand the district's green spaces. For now, he continues his work with the resources available to him, identifying suitable locations, raising saplings, watering them and ensuring that they survive.
At 56, his journey offers a refreshing perspective on environmental activism. It does not always require a massive campaign, expensive machinery or institutional backing to begin making a difference. Sometimes, it starts with noticing a problem on a familiar road, planting a few saplings and returning every day with a bucket of water. Nearly 10,000 trees later, Chinna's efforts have turned that small act of concern into a mission that continues to benefit people, animals and the environment.

title: India warns against using tech for strategic one-upmanship, calls for inclusive AI governance
description: India urges inclusive AI governance, warns against tech-driven strategic abuse, and protect human oversight in lethal autonomous weapons.
author: PTI
content:
India has voiced concern over the instrumentalisation of technology for strategic one-upmanship through export control and licensing regimes, calling out the tendency to treat countries of the Global South as mere consumers as it underscored that technological transformation must not deepen existing inequalities.
Addressing the Security Council’s high-level open debate on Maintenance of International Peace and Security on ‘Conflict Resolution in an Era of Rapid Technological Change’, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni said AI systems can inadvertently perpetuate biases related to gender, language and socio-economic background.
“We note with concern the emerging medium- and long-term trends of technology denial and the instrumentalisation of technology for strategic one-upmanship through export control and licensing regimes, and a tendency to treat countries of the Global South as mere consumers without any agency or stake in how emerging technologies such as AI are developed, are regulated and are deployed,” Mr. Parvathaneni said.
“AI must not reduce human beings to mere data points or raw material. India supports inclusive international cooperation on technology governance, including through the United Nations, with due regard to national priorities and developmental needs,” he said.
He emphasised that technology should serve humanity, strengthen international cooperation, and advance the cause of lasting peace.
“Technology may inform human judgement but cannot and should not replace it,” he said.
India also asserted that amid the rapid integration of artificial intelligence into military and intelligence spheres, responsibility for use of lethal autonomous weapons systems must always rest with humans.
“Rapid technological advances are fundamentally transforming the nature of conflict and the international security landscape. Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, and emerging digital technologies present unprecedented opportunities but also introduce new vulnerabilities and risks across the entire conflict cycle,” Mr. Parvathaneni said.
He added that the rapid integration of artificial intelligence into military, intelligence, and civilian spheres has fundamentally transformed the landscape of international peace and security.
India stressed that the application of emerging technologies in conflict settings must be responsible, human-centric, respect sovereignty, and adhere to international law.
“Emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems raise legitimate legal and ethical questions. India is committed to addressing these within the framework of the Convention on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), which seeks to balance military necessity with humanitarian considerations,” Mr. Parvathaneni said.
He underscored that human judgement and oversight remain essential, taking into account the operational context and characteristics of the weapons system. “Responsibility for the use of such systems must always rest with humans,” the Indian envoy said, adding that leveraging technology for protection must be a cross-cutting and cross-sectoral measure.
“It must be used for the protection of civilians and of peacekeepers and should be leveraged for the protection of humanitarian personnel.”
India called on the international community to address threats posed by misuse of emerging technologies such as AI.
“The risks associated with AI are real, and we must address them without any hesitation. The potential misuse of these emerging technologies by terrorists and non-State actors is a matter of grave concern. Incomplete, inaccurate, or deliberately manipulated data through AI can undermine decision-making,” he said.
He told the Council that India has made robust advancements in digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies, reflecting a clear emphasis on protecting critical information infrastructure and ensuring the continuity of essential civilian services.
Addressing the Security Council Open Debate, Secretary General Antonio Guterres voiced concern that today’s wars have become “proving grounds” for AI-enabled targeting.
Asserting that killer robots must have no place in the world’s future, Mr. Guterres reiterated his call to urgently launch negotiations for a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems.
“AI is driving greater autonomy across military functions. From intelligence gathering to target selection, it is reported that algorithms are increasingly shaping life-and-death decisions,” he said, adding that these capabilities are within the reach of both States and non-State armed groups.
“And the potential integration of AI with nuclear command, control and communication systems is a recipe for catastrophe. As long as nuclear weapons exist, the decision to use them must rest with human beings alone,” Mr. Guterres said.
“When civilians are killed, or human rights are violated, the answer must never be ‘the algorithm did it’,” Mr. Guterres said.
The UN chief added that humans must always retain control over life-and-death decisions – guided by international law and ethical principles.
“Technology companies must reckon with the legal risks they may face if their services contribute to violations of international law. And no country should design, develop, deploy, or use military applications of AI in armed conflict that violate international law, international humanitarian law, or international human rights law,” he said.

title: Tamil Nadu government set to ink 70 MoUs for investments to the tune of over ₹50,000 crore
description: Tamil Nadu to sign 70+ MoUs worth over ₹50,000 crore across manufacturing, energy, textiles, aerospace, and defence at a Chennai conclave.
author: Sangeetha Kandavel
content:
Tamil Nadu is set to sign over 70 memoranda of understanding (MoUs), entailing investments of over Rs. 50,000 crore, at the VETTRI Tamil Nadu Investment and Conversion Conclave, scheduled to be held in Chennai on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).
Sources said the MoUs would cover sectors including manufacturing, clean energy, textiles, aerospace and defence.
It is learnt that Royal Enfield will be signing a deal for EV motorbikes.
Keppel-backed Cleantech Solar, a renewable energy developer with a portfolio of 1.2 MWp+ renewable energy projects, including over 400 MW in Tamil Nadu, is also signing a deal. This will be a five-year investment, integrating solar, wind and battery energy storage systems, designed to meet the evolving energy requirements of Tamil Nadu’s commercial and industrial sectors.
Sources say the two South Korean automotive component manufacturers — Seoyon E-Hwa Summit Automotive India Private Limited and Hwashin Automotive India Private Limited — that recently expressed interest in investing in Tamil Nadu will also be signing MoUs.
“Turning investment intent into working facilities and steady livelihoods is what matters most for our people. Our focus is on practical execution, responsive institutions, and balanced industrial growth across Tamil Nadu,” Industries Minister S. Keerthana said.
Status report
The TVK government will also provide an update on the MoUs signed since the party came to power, including the number of project proposals that have translated into actual investments. It will also present a status report on the remaining projects, detailing their progress at various stages, such as land acquisition and construction.
At its first investors’ conclave held in August this year, the TVK government signed 97 MoUs, entailing more than Rs. 67,542 crore in investments.

title: Delhi wakes up to coldest morning of the season; Air quality ‘poor’
description: Delhi endures coldest morning of the season as air quality stays poor with several very poor readings and sub-15°C lows.
author: PTI
content:
Delhi recorded its coldest morning of the season on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), with the minimum temperature settling at 10°C.
The minimum temperature at Safdarjung, the city's base weather station, was 1.3° below the season's normal, while it dropped by 1.2° degrees compared to the previous day.
Air quality in Delhi remained in the ‘poor’ category, with four monitoring stations recording 'very poor' readings, even as the city's average Air Quality Index (AQI) stood at 224.
The total number of weather stations active at 9:05 a.m. was 56 out of the total 59 in the city.
Other parts of the city also recorded relatively low temperatures. Lodhi Road recorded a minimum of 10.1°C, followed by Ayanagar at 10.4° , Palam at 11° and the Ridge at 11.7°.
The minimum temperature at Palam remained unchanged from Tuesday (November 24), while Lodhi Road recorded a drop of 0.6°. The Ridge saw a fall of 0.3° degrees, while Ayanagar recorded a marginal rise of 0.2°.
No rainfall was recorded at any of the five weather stations during the 24 hours ending at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday (November 25).
According to the CPCB, an AQI between 0 and 50 is classified as 'good', 51 and 100 as 'satisfactory', 101 and 200 as 'moderate', 201 and 300 as 'poor', 301 and 400 as 'very poor', and 401 and 500 as 'severe'.
The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecasted shallow fog for the day, and the maximum temperature is likely to touch 25°C.

title: Government examining measures to curb human-elephant conflict in Hassan, says Forest Minister
description: The State government is examining a series of measures to address the growing problem of human-elephant conflict in Hassan district, including the installation of steel-rope barricades and fitting GPS collars on elephants to monitor their movements, Minister for Forest, Ecology and Environment Ramalinga Reddy said on Tuesday.
author: The Hindu Bureau
content:
The State government is examining a series of measures to address the growing problem of human-elephant conflict in Hassan district, including the installation of steel-rope barricades and fitting GPS collars on elephants to monitor their movements, Minister for Forest, Ecology and Environment Ramalinga Reddy said on Tuesday.
The Minister said residents of Belur, Sakleshpur and other parts of Hassan district have been facing difficulties owing to elephant movement, and the State government was taking their concerns seriously.
The Minister was speaking to presspersons after inaugurating the new main entrance gate and various development works at the Atal Bihari Vajpayee Zoological Park at Kamalapura near Hampi in Vijayanagara district. The works were taken up at a cost of ₹18 crore with assistance from the Vijayanagara District Mineral Foundation and other sources. He also laid the foundation stone for additional works estimated to cost ₹3 crore.
Pointing to the fragmented nature of forest areas in the region, he said nearly 13,000 acres of forest in Belur taluk were spread across nine separate patches, and the nearly one lakh acres of forest area in Sakleshpur were similarly divided into more than 80 patches. “This fragmentation made it difficult to regulate elephant movement and prevent human-elephant conflict,” he said.
The proposal to relocate elephants to the Bhadra forest area had been under discussion for some time, and the government would also take into consideration the concerns expressed by local elected representatives, Mr. Reddy said.
“The feasibility of installing steel-rope barricades to prevent elephants from straying out of forests is being examined, subject to financial constraints. A plan to fit GPS collars on elephants and continuously monitor their movements was also being implemented,” he said.
Kamalapur zoo development
Speaking on the development initiatives taken at the Atal Bihari Vajpayee Zoological Park at Kamalapura near Hampi in Vijayanagara district, Mr. Reddy said that several facilities have been developed at the zoo with funding from the Vijayanagara District Mineral Foundation, the Karnataka Mining Environment Restoration Corporation and contributions from mining companies.
“Hampi is an important historical destination that attracts a large number of tourists. The government is committed to developing the zoo as an additional attraction,” he said.
The Minister said that arrangements had been made to ensure an uninterrupted supply of water, fodder and food for the animals and birds. Solar-powered borewells had been installed to ensure a regular water supply and to meet emergency requirements. Shade had also been provided for the animals, while a sprinkler system had been introduced to maintain the plants.
The zoo would be provided with additional animal species, with priority given to their health and conservation, he said. New open and closed jeeps and buses had also been arranged to facilitate safari tours.
K.S. Basavanthappa, Vijayanagara district in-charge Minister; H.R. Gaviyappa, Hosapete MLA; E. Tukaram, Ballari MP; M.P. Latha Mallikarjun, Harapanahalli MLA; K. Rangaswamy, Karnataka Zoo Authority chairman; Kavita Mannikeri, Deputy Commissioner; S. Jahnavi, Superintendent of Police; and senior forest department officials were present.

title: Witness protection essential to criminal justice system: Kerala HC
description: Kerala High Court stresses witness protection as essential to justice, orders timely BNSS scheme implementation and protection for approver Muhammed Asmin.
author: The Hindu Bureau
content:
The Kerala High Court has observed that the protection of witnesses is not merely a matter of individual security but an essential prerequisite for effective administration of justice.
The Division Bench of Justices Raja Vijayaraghavan and K.V. Jayakumar held that a system which expected witnesses to come forward and assisted the investigation should also ensure their safety. The court thus granted bail to a Sri Lankan national, Muhammed Asmin, who had turned approver in an alleged transnational conspiracy to revive the banned terrorist organisation, the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) through drugs and arms trafficking.The matter came to light when 300 kg of heroin, AK-47 rifles and 1,000 rounds of ammunition were seized.
The court observed that Mr. Asmin had spent four years as an undertrial prisoner, and it would be unjust to continue his incarceration any longer given that he was granted a pardon previously by the NIA Special Court, Chennai.
Mr. Asmin was accused of facilitating the movement of drug consignments, handling the proceeds of unlawful transactions through hawala channels and converting the proceeds of crime into cryptocurrency. He had received the pardon from the Special Court after agreeing to cooperate with the investigation and fully disclose all his knowledge concerning the alleged offences and other accused. However the court had refused to release him on bail, insisting that continued custody of an approver served the dual purpose of protecting his life and personal safety from possible reprisals at the hands of his former associates and ensuring that the course of justice remains unpolluted by any attempt to influence, intimidate or win him over before he enters the witness box.
The High Court clarified that the Special Court was not justified in rejecting Ms. Asmin’s bail citing a rule that was not applicable to him under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court further pointed out that the fundamental rights of the accused should be protected when a trial was prolonged.
The court directed that the Kerala Witness Protection Scheme should be implemented without delay to provide security to witnesses as envisioned under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). The court noted that a draft Scheme was currently under consideration of the State government. The court observed that Mr. Asmin should be considered for protection under the Scheme, in view of his role as an approver and his decision to assist the prosecution by giving evidence against the other accused.

title: Meerut Police arrest 22-year-old man for plotting to carry out suicide attacks on Army camp
description: Meerut police arrest 22-year-old linked to Pakistan-backed online network plotting suicide attack on Army camp.
author: PTI
content:
Meerut Police have arrested a 22-year-old absconding man linked to a Pakistan-backed online radicalisation network on charges of plotting to carry out a ‘fidayeen’ (suicide) attack on an Army camp, officials said on Tuesday (November 24, 2026).
Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) BBGTS Murthy told reporters at the Reserve Police Lines that the arrested individual was identified as Uzaid, a resident of Baniyapada in Meerut.
He was arrested in a joint operation by the Kotwali police and the SWAT team.
The accused allegedly used to consume ‘anti-India’ content on Instagram and YouTube and was influenced by Masood Azhar, the chief of Pakistan-based terror group Jaish-e-Mohammed.
According to police, Uzaid was in touch with a Jammu-based resident, Mohammad Sajid, and both were running the online network, which was backed by Pakistani gangster Shahzad Bhatti.
The network was allegedly involved in radicalising youths in India to carry out suicide attacks on military installations.
The case came to light on November 24, 2025, after a complaint was registered at Bahu Fort police station in Jammu in connection with terror-related activities, following which Sajid was arrested.
Sajid’s arrest led Jammu and Meerut police to conduct joint raids in Meerut in search of Uzaid in January 2026 and again in February 2026. However, he had absconded.
A police officer said that after Uzaid absconded, the Meerut Senior Superintendent of Police directed the formation of a team under the Superintendent of Police (City).
“He was arrested from Gahlot Road in the Kotwali police station area following a tip-off by the informers. The accused was absconding for 10 months. During this period, he would sometimes stay at his mama’s (maternal uncle’s) place and sometimes at any other location,” the officer told PTI.
Police said that during interrogation, Uzaid allegedly admitted to consuming “anti-India” content on Instagram and YouTube.
“He also watched and listened to videos by Maulana Masood Azhar (a Pakistani terrorist), Tariq Masood, and Israr Ahmed,” police said.
He had come into contact with Sajid after commenting “hum bhi taiyaar hain” (we are also ready) on one of his videos.
According to the police, both had hatched a plan to carry out a ‘fidayeen’ attack on a major Army camp in November 2025.
Under this plan, Sajid was tasked with conducting reconnaissance, while Uzaid was responsible for procuring weapons and explosive-laden vests.
Police also claimed that there was a plan to facilitate the delivery of weapons and provide training via the Gurez Valley route. But the plan didn’t materialise after Sajid was arrested.
Police further said both were running online groups called ‘Tuition-40’, ‘Brigade’ and ‘Al-Muzzahid’ on Instagram and the ‘Session’ messaging app to radicalise youth.
Police claimed that Uzaid played a key role in managing these groups and remained in contact with Sajid using Instagram, Session, and the Signal app.
They further said a case has been registered against Sajjad at the Bahu Fort police station in Jammu under Section 113(3) (Terrorist Act) of the BNS.
Meerut Police said that Jammu Police has been informed of Uzaid’s arrest and is on the way to question him. Police are currently investigating other suspects and contacts linked to the alleged terror network.

title: Former members say EPG report was ‘highly positive’ for India-Nepal ties
description: Former EPG member calls the India-Nepal report highly positive, contrasting with Misri’s “not relevant” stance and urging unveiled bilateral progress.
author: Kallol Bhattacherjee
content:
A day after Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri termed the report of the India-Nepal Eminent Persons Group (EPG) “not relevant”, arguing that India will take a “forward looking” approach regarding boundary issues with Nepal, a former member of the EPG has said the report was “highly positive” for both India and Nepal and that it was “odd” that the group did not get a chance to present the report to the Government of India.
“The EPG report was produced after extensive research and field visits. We visited Visakhapatnam and other ports that are of interest to Nepal and spoke with many stakeholders before compiling the report and there are interesting recommendations in the report that could be of great use for India and Nepal and it was highly positive for Delhi-Kathmandu relations,” said Mahendra P. Lama, former professor of Jawaharlal Nehru University, who served as a member of the EPG.
ALSO WATCH India-Nepal ties: What does Modi-Balen partnership promise? | Above the Fold | Nov 23, 2026
The EPG returned to the spotlight on Monday (November 23, 2026) when Mr. Misri announced in a press conference held after the visit of Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah that New Delhi would adopt a “forward-looking” approach to the border issues. “The leaders have given a direction as part of the overall very forward-looking discussions that have been held today for the foreign secretaries to take the task forward. We will do so in a forward-looking manner, taking inspiration from the vision document and from the directions and indeed the spirit in which the discussions were held. I would say that EPG is in the past. We are not looking backward,” said Mr. Misri in response to a question. He described the EPG report as “not relevant”.
‘Not unilateral document’
Former Nepali ambassador and coordinator of the EPG on the Nepali side, Bhek Bahadur Thapa, described the EPG report as a step forward for the bilateral consultation process. “It was not a unilateral document, it was a document created through bilateral consultation among experts appointed by New Delhi and Kathmandu,” said Mr. Thapa, who has also served as Foreign Minister of Nepal during 2004-05. The EPG report dealing with a broad spectrum of India-Nepal relations, including the Kalapani dispute and the 1950 India-Nepal Friendship Treaty was completed in 2018 but it remained under sealed covers. “It is odd that the report could not be launched here in Delhi. The Nepali side said the EPG report should be unveiled first by the Indian Prime Minister and on the same day we were supposed to return to Kathmandu for the report’s unveiling by the Nepali Prime Minister, “ said Prof. Lama, informing that they made a mistake as Kathmandu could have also unveiled the report first. “Our recommendations now can be accessed by other stakeholders in Kathmandu and I don’t think that is a positive thing,” said Mr. Lama.
The EPG was institutionalised according to an understanding that was reached during the delegation-level talks between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and former Nepali Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli in February 2016. The visit of Mr. Oli took place against the backdrop of months-long blockade on Nepal-India border that Kathmandu said was imposed by India but India blamed the Madhesi agitators of Nepal for imposing the blockade that hindered flow of essential items such as cooking gas into Nepal. During the time of its existence, a part of the Institute of Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA) in Delhi served as the secretariat for the EPG. The then Director General of the IDSA Jayant Prasad was also part of the EPG.
Incidentally, officials who are currently playing key roles in India-Nepal relations were also involved in the EPG process. Former members recounted that the newly appointed Indian ambassador to Nepal Sudhakar Dalela was the Joint Secretary (North) in the Ministry of External Affairs and was part of the EPG process during 2016-18. That apart, the new Nepali ambassador to India Nischal Nath Pandey also was part of the EPG process in Kathmandu.

title: No defence data breach, says Government, as security agencies asked to audit messaging groups
description: Govt says no defence data breach; security agencies audit messaging groups amid cyber-safety talks and warnings about sensitive info on apps.
author: Saurabh Trivedi
content:
There has been no leak of sensitive information pertaining to the Defence Forces, a senior Defence Ministry official said on Tuesday (November 24, 2026), even as security establishments reiterated advisories against sharing sensitive data on messaging applications.
The official said documents circulating on social media claiming to contain defence-related information were fake and intended to create confusion.
However, an advisory has been issued to all formations, directing personnel to exercise caution while using messaging platforms.
“The documents pertaining to the Defence Forces circulating on social media are fake and have been developed to create chaos. There is no data leak. There is a strict advisory that no sensitive information, in any form, should be shared or discussed on messaging apps,” the official said.
A high-level meeting has been convened at the Ministry of Home Affairs on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) to discuss issues related to data breaches and cyber safety.
The developments come amid reports that Pakistan-based Intelligence Operatives (PIOs) have infiltrated unofficial WhatsApp groups used by Indian defence, paramilitary and civil defence personnel to gather sensitive information.
An advisory issued last week to defence and security establishments, including the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), flagged attempts by PIOs to gain unauthorised access to WhatsApp groups using spoofed or compromised mobile numbers.
The operatives were allegedly functioning as "silent members" in these groups to monitor conversations and collect information.
The advisory covers the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force (BSF), Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) and Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), among other establishments.
Group administrators have been directed to conduct audits of membership lists and remove unknown and unverified members.
Security personnel have also been asked to organise cyber awareness campaigns to improve vigilance against such attempts, the offical said.
The Defence Forces have an indigenous messaging application for secure communication, the official said, reiterating that sensitive information must not be shared through unofficial platforms.
Recently, the Ministry of Defence issued an advisory directing military personnel, including soldiers and officers, to refrain from using 87 mobile applications over concerns about data security and the potential misuse of sensitive information.
Separately, Delhi Police detained a 14-year-old boy from Palwal, in Haryana, over alleged attempts to sell Agniveer-related data on the dark web.
The data was purportedly sourced from a Ministry of Home Affairs test portal. Records relating to around 2,500 individuals were recovered for verification.
